extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political science, criminology, and modern British political history
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe features by which a state moves toward an 'exceptional' law-and-order form — legislative tightening, mobilisation of enforcement agencies, and ideological convergence on 'violence' (UK, early 1970s case studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 — Overwhelming legislative tendency toward the law
rubrics_metrics.description: The state moves 'in the direction of the law' via a sheer comprehensiveness of supporting legislative activity, culminating in a tightening of legal sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Industrial Relations Act (direct attack on organised labour), Misuse of Drugs Act (linking possession to harmfulness and raising trafficking penalties), Criminal Damage Act (broad offence of damage without lawful excuse, high maximum penalties), Immigration Act (strict controls on Commonwealth immigration). The text emphasises that this legislative avalanche is staggering and forms the first phase of institutionalising a law-and-order panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 — Mobilisation and extended routine use of law-enforcement agencies for 'informal' control
rubrics_metrics.description: The extended, routine employment of police and security agencies to exercise informal control across social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific practices: activating Special Squads and Special Branch, increased surveillance and information‑gathering, dawn raids, heavy questioning, use of 'verbals' (statements that leave doubts when used in court), restrictions on freedom of assembly, strong policing of demonstrations, free use of warrants, sweeping suspected charges against whole groups, and collection/seizure of literature and private documents. These measures are described as an 'anticipatory' use of police and part of a more-than-routine repressive apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 3 — Ideological convergence at the 'violence' threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency for disparate issues and threats to be ideologically reframed so they converge at a 'violence' threshold, justifying exceptional responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by militaristic framing (Brigadier Kitson's Low Intensity Operations) distinguishing civil disturbance, insurgency, guerrilla warfare, subversion, terrorism, civil disobedience etc., and encouraging army counter‑insurgency roles. The convergence around 'violence' supplies the narrative that legitimates exceptional legal and policing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of legal instruments to discipline labour and suppress industrial action
rubrics_metrics.description: Deployment of statutory measures and judicial institutions to contain, discipline, and undermine organised labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Industrial Relations Act required union registration with fines, undermined the closed shop, defined a wide ambiguous area of 'unfair industrial practices' (strikes), imposed delays and legal risks on withdrawal of labour, and established the Industrial Relations Court as the 'engine' for disciplined reform. The state also used exemplary arrests and prosecutions to make examples of key sectors (power workers, Post Office, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Toughening of legal administration and judicial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardening in the practical administration of law: longer and exemplary sentences, strategic use of bail and costs, administrative extensions of law, and biases in judicial interpretation favoring police/prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described consequences include discouraging accused persons from robust defence, widening the arm of the law through administrative procedures, and an overall erosion of civil liberties, judicial equality and the rule of law under the pressure of raison d'etat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tribunals, secret hearings and suspension of legal protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Recourse to extra-judicial or exceptional procedures that curtail normal legal protections and oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rudi Dutschke tried before a tribunal (not a court), tribunal secret sessions excluding defendant and counsel and relying on unnamed witnesses; scrapping of immigration appeals procedure for political militants; Emergency Powers Act (internment) making the army quasi‑judicial in Northern Ireland; later occasional suspension of habeas corpus and the Prevention of Terrorism Act. These measures blur the line between legal and arbitrary repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalisation via broadly framed new statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: New statutory definitions and penalties that criminalise a wide range of conduct, bringing protests, squats and dissent within criminal law's shadow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misuse of Drugs Act linked possession to alleged harmfulness and imposed severe trafficking penalties; Criminal Damage Act redefined offences as damage to property without lawful excuse with maximum penalties (ten years, 'aggravated damage' carrying life recommendation), thereby potentially encompassing squatting, picketing and demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of specialised surveillance/intelligence units outside parliamentary oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation and growth of intelligence and information‑coordinating units within policing and Home Office structures, operating with limited parliamentary control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: establishment of National Immigration Intelligence Unit and National Drugs Intelligence Unit; expansion of surveillance, record‑keeping and co‑ordination by the Home Office and Scotland Yard. Home Office Ministers characterised some activities as 'operational activities of the police ... not normally subject to Parliamentary control.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Law used as instrument of censorship and moral regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Deployment of obscenity and public‑morals law, police squads and prosecutions to police culture and suppress counter‑cultural publications and performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: Obscene Publications Act let enforcement be tightened (Obscene Publications Squad raids on underground press, seizure of printers' files); prosecutions/convictions of Little Red Schoolbook, International Times, Oz (schoolchildren's issue), seizure of Warhol's Flesh. Moral campaign organisations (National Viewers and Listeners Association, Mrs Whitehouse) and establishment committees (Longford Committee) fed into legal and cultural repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilisation of moral guardians and populist reaction to legitimate repression
rubrics_metrics.description: Alignment of populist moral campaigns, media narratives and establishment figures with legal repression to create a law‑and‑order crusade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Festival of Light marches, prominent voices like Lord Hailsham, Lord Longford, Malcolm Muggeridge, and media framings that presented unions and counter‑culture figures as threats to 'decent' society. The text stresses how moral outrage moved from fringe to mainstream and meshed with legal enforcement to legitimate repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing dissent as 'conspiracy' to justify extraordinary measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking the notion of conspiracy as the organising legal and ideological framework that legitimates undermining checks and balances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that the idea of conspiracy was used to justify a steady 'corruption of the formal checks and balances' — the belief that 'conspiracy must be met by conspiracy' under the rubric of raison d'etat — producing legal innovations and covert procedures directed at political militants and suspected 'urban terrorism'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racialised and immigration‑focused legal repression
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and policing measures that codify and normalise discriminatory practices against immigrant and racialised communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 1971 Immigration Act is described as formalising earlier anti‑immigrant street practices (search on suspicion, raids on black clubs), exempting 'Old Commonwealth' whites and making entry conditional/contractual for male labour while disproportionately harming women, children and families. The legislation was accompanied by sweeps of immigrant communities and aggressive local policing.
